PASS for business-analysis feasibility: multiple current routes let independent agencies access commercial/trucking markets, including trucking-specific partner/MGA access. External signup, appetite confirmation and contracts are execution steps and remain owner-gated.

PASS for legal-path feasibility: Illinois has a defined P&C producer/business-entity licensing route, renewal/CE framework, and defined bond rule for brokered placements. Actual licensure/E&O/bond/appointments remain launch prerequisites, not analysis prerequisites.

PASS for research-stage beachhead strength: the project has an owner-confirmed ~40-contact trucking network. Under conservative fixed-cost/commission scenarios, only 3-6 binds (7.5%-15% of that network) are needed to cover stressed fixed infrastructure before service labor. Generic insurance benchmarks are used only as a plausibility check. Actual network response belongs to measured_channel_response market validation.

PASS for structural scale path: beyond the initial ~40-contact network, current trucking-agency infrastructure offers renewal-book management and scalable lead flow, while public carrier/renewal data can support prospecting. These are not unique advantages and CAC remains unvalidated, so acquisition_cac and competition_wedge stay open.

FAIL as a standalone business at the currently evidenced channel scale: basic repair/protection referrals pay about $100-$250 per funded/sold event; factoring can create lifetime residuals, but public 2025 program economics do not establish enough revenue per owned-network contact to support a standalone company without much larger distribution.

PASS for structural repeat/LTV: independent P&C compensation explicitly includes renewal commissions, a current trucking producer program pays on renewals, and trucking market-access tooling is built around renewal books. Actual retention rate remains an input to unit economics, not a question of whether recurring revenue exists.

PASS for launch feasibility with two people: current trucking-agency infrastructure is sold to one-user startups, current producer roles demonstrate one licensed producer can originate/service a trucking book with agency tooling, and industry service-capacity benchmarks are far above the initial ~40-contact beachhead. Exact service minutes remain in unit-economics validation.
After owner-approved external validation, measure contacted/qualified/quoted/bound funnel in the actual owned trucking network.
After owner-approved external validation, calculate cash + owner-time acquisition cost per quote and per bound account.
After owner-approved external validation, calculate actual commission received minus market-access fees, E&O allocation, servicing/endorsement/COI/remarketing labor and other direct costs.

PASS for research-stage acquisition feasibility: first-channel cash lead cost is near-zero because the network is already owned/known; modeled fixed-cost coverage requires 3-6 binds from ~40 contacts. TIS/public market channels provide expansion options. Actual response, owner-time CAC and cost per bound account remain empirical market-validation gates.

PASS for research-stage unit-economics feasibility: account gross-commission scenarios are large relative to bounded fixed startup costs. Even a deliberately heavy ~$5.27k fixed-cost stress case requires 3-6 binds at modeled $2,250-$960 gross commission. This does NOT prove net profit; actual service labor, exact commission contract, E&O quote and net contribution are reserved for measured_net_contribution market validation.

PASS narrowly for research-stage entry wedge, not product differentiation: local trucking specialists are strong and language/trucking expertise are not unique. The surviving wedge is privileged warm access to an existing ~40-contact carrier/driver network combined with broad market-access feasibility, giving the new entrant a credible reason to obtain quote opportunities without buying cold leads. Whether buyers actually choose/bind is an empirical market-validation question.
PASS: current Chicago-area and national providers charge recurring $149-$499+ for owner-operator/small-fleet compliance and software substitutes also command recurring spend.

PASS for research-stage two-person feasibility: provider/partner infrastructure can absorb major workflow components, and conservative sensitivity bounds a 10-account starting book at <=20 routine service hours/month if standardized scope stays <=2 hours/account. A 20-account book is <=40 routine hours/month. Actual onboarding, exceptions and service minutes remain empirical inputs.

PASS for research-stage unit economics, not realized profit: 10 accounts x $199/month with a conservative $499/month backend and $50/hour labor yields about $491/month (~24.7%) before other overhead at 2 routine service hours/account and breaks even near 3 hours/account. Current $149-$499 managed-service pricing and lower-cost backend/substitute components support a credible positive-contribution path. Actual labor, liability, vendor terms and retention remain measured_net_contribution inputs.

PASS for research-stage acquisition feasibility: initial channel is an existing warm trucking network. Cash CAC can be low; actual owner-time CAC remains empirical.

PASS for research-stage two-person feasibility: current practice-capacity benchmarks put light monthly clients around 3-4 hours and standard clients around 5-8, with roughly 15-30 monthly clients per solo bookkeeper depending on depth. A 10-20 account launch book is structurally feasible for two people if recurring scope is standardized and cleanup is separately priced/scheduled. Actual trucking-specific hours remain empirical.

PASS for research-stage unit-economics feasibility, not profit forecast: at $350/month, a $50/account software/admin allowance and $50/hour direct labor leave ~$100/month contribution at 4 recurring hours and ~$50 at 5 hours; break-even is about 6 hours. At $500/month, 6 hours leaves ~$150 (~30%). Current providers publish $300-$500+ owner-operator pricing, while low-price substitutes show that full-service scope must not be sold as commodity bookkeeping. Actual hours, review cost, cleanup and retention remain measured_net_contribution inputs.
